title: Repentance unto Life - Part One
speaker: Mr. Nick Newton
summary: This lesson explores the doctrine of repentance unto life as presented in Chapter 15 of the Westminster Confession of Faith. Mr. Newton defines repentance through Scripture and theological reflection, contrasting true repentance (which leads to salvation) with the sorrow of the world (which leads to death), and establishes repentance as an essential gospel grace that must be preached alongside faith in Christ.

outline.title: Definition and Nature of Repentance unto Life
subpoints: Repentance involves changing one's mind and purpose, expressing regret and lament, and turning away from sin toward God's mercy
True repentance leads to heart and life change, not merely confession or remorse
Distinguished from the sorrow of the world, which leads to death (exemplified by Judas)

outline.title: Repentance as an Evangelical Grace (Paragraph 1)
subpoints: Repentance unto life is a gospel grace—a gift integral to God's plan of salvation
This grace is distributed to all the elect under the New Covenant, both Jews and Gentiles
Repentance must be preached by every minister of the gospel alongside faith in Christ

outline.title: Repentance and Confession Distinguished
subpoints: Confession is an action of owning sin but lacks the necessary heart orientation
True repentance requires both confession and a genuine turning from sin
Teaching full repentance, not merely confession, is critical from the pulpit

outline.title: Repentance Not as Satisfaction for Sin (Paragraph 3)
subpoints: Repentance is not the cause of pardon; Christ's sacrifice alone satisfies sin
Yet repentance is of such necessity that none may expect pardon without it
Repentance must accompany faith—faith without repentance is falsehood, repentance without faith is fruitless
God grants repentance not because our changed attitudes impress Him, but out of His mercy

outline.title: The Scope of Divine Mercy (Paragraph 4)
subpoints: No sin is so small that it does not deserve damnation
No sin is so great that it brings damnation upon those who truly repent
God's holiness requires judgment, but His mercy freely forgives those who genuinely repent
True repentance results in God's healing, free love, and new life in the believer

outline.title: The Necessity and Hope of Repentance
subpoints: Without a repentant heart, faith is effectively lifeless
Repentance is as essential to Christian life as the breathing lung is to the body
God's grace in repentance brings not merely pardon but healing, renewal, and transformation

transcript:
## Opening Remarks

It is an honor to have been asked to join in this series on the Westminster Confession of Faith. First John 1:9, we've all heard this. It goes:

> "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

God doesn't just hear us repent. He doesn't just give us a thumbs up and go on with his day. He immediately picks up the ledger of our soul and transfers the debt of the sin we repent of to the ledger of his son's infinite crucifixion secured grace. Really, it's a gift within a gift. We have the privilege of repentance and wrapped up within that is new life.

We'll be looking at that through the lens of Chapter 15 of the Westminster Confession of Faith. This week, I will attempt to define the idea of repentance unto life. I believe it's page 856 and 57 in your hymnal through the lens of Scripture as the divines are envisioning it. Then next week, we'll break down what it looks like to strive for true repentance and the place it ought to have in our walks. We'll be looking at it in the public and private applications in our lives.

I've leaned pretty heavily on Chad Vendixhorn's Confessing the Faith, which was used for our book study, but I'd recommend it to all of you if you're seeking to study the doctrines of the confession. It's very well put together and very all-encompassing. I've also used J.G. Vos's larger catechism commentary as the larger catechism is a smaller synopsis of the truths of the confession. I definitely praise the Lord for men that are more learned than I am in that department. There would be a lot of preaching to myself in this one. I've long struggled with a proper mindset on repentance and I'm thankful for the spurring to study this chapter and focus on it. I pray that this will be profitable for you guys as well.

## What Does Repentance unto Life Mean?

The heading in the hymnal there is "repentance unto life." So what does that mean? What does that even mean anyways?

2 Corinthians 7:10 goes:

> "For godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, not to be regretted, but the sorrow of the world produces death."

Right out the gate, Paul is making a distinction between a repentance that leads to life and a repentance that leads to death. Repentance unto salvation we know is eternal life in the presence of our holy God, the most perfect and wholesome life we could ever conceive of. I'm going to continue referring to 2 Corinthians 7 quite a bit this week and next. It'll be a sort of a core passage for these couple lessons.

### Definition of Repentance

The King James Dictionary offers a two-part definition of the word repentance. When you string them end to end, it produces kind of a four-step picture or path to true repentance. Part one is to change one's mind and purpose and regret. The second part is to lament one's actions and turn again.

So to change one's mind and purpose and regret, and lament one's actions and to turn again. Once we're convicted with our sin presented before our hearts and minds, we identify the problem. We then reorient our desires and goals or our mind and purpose to oppose the identified sin. Subsequently we express grief on two fronts: regret and lament, with regret being the internal within our hearts and conscience and lament being the external as we speak with God about our affronts to his holiness. The final step is turning again. We turn once to the sin that we're now confronting and repenting of. We turn again, this time to the mercy and grace given to us through Christ's accomplishment on the cross, that we might be strengthened against that sin in the future and live a life that glorifies God more.

### True Repentance Leads to Life Change

True repentance leads to heart and life change. The idea of repentance throughout Scripture is coupled with exhortations and examples of altering behavior. True repentance ought to be accompanied by sincere volition to live in ways that further God's glory and not sins. We find a lot of these proof texts accompanying chapter 15 in this regard.

Ezekiel 14:6:

> "Therefore say to the house of Israel, thus says the Lord, repent, turn away from your idols and turn your faces away from all your abominations."

Ezekiel 18:30:

> "Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, everyone according to his ways, says the Lord, repent and turn from all your transgressions so that the iniquity will not be your ruin."

Mark 1:15:

> "The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is at hand, repent and believe in the gospel."

Acts 3:19:

> "Repent, therefore, and be convicted that your sins may be blotted out so that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord."

Acts 26:20:

> "Declared first to those in Damascus and in Jerusalem throughout all the region of Judea, then to the Gentiles, that they should repent, turn to God, and do works befitting of repentance."

### The Antithetical Doctrine: Repentance unto Death

Now to better understand the idea of repentance unto life, I think we should examine the antithetical doctrine of the sorrow of the world, or as J.G. Vos puts it, repentance unto death. In his commentary on the larger catechism, he uses the case of Judas' suicide along with Paul's writing in 2 Corinthians that we just read a moment ago to illustrate this distinction.

We read that Judas repented himself and hanged himself. That's Matthew 27:3-5 in the King James Version. This false repentance is also called the sorrow of the world, 2 Corinthians 7:10, in contrast to true repentance or godly sorrow. There we read that the sorrow of the world worketh death, that is to say it is not repentance unto life, but repentance unto death, for the outcome is not eternal life, but eternal death.

So Judas was overcome with the sorrow of the world. He was sorry that he did it and understood it was wrong. His conscience brought him to his knees in a flash flood of guilt. His conscience being so seared though it pointed him not to his savior, but to his noose. The only response his heart could muster to rid himself of guilt was to go out on his own terms. That's a graphic example, but it demonstrates that undirected remorse in place of repentance to God leads to death.

I'll pick a bone with Vos here and say that repentance unto death then is a contradiction in terms. We can't expect life to spring up from a flood of guilt not aimed towards the source of new life.

## Diving into the Confession: Paragraph One

With a basic understanding of what the Westminster Assembly was getting at here with the terms of repentance and new life, let's dive into the confession and fold the doctrine further. We'll start with paragraph one and then we'll be bouncing to paragraphs three and four for this week and we'll cover the remaining three next week.

### Repentance unto Life as an Evangelical Grace

**Paragraph One:** "Repentance unto life is an evangelical grace. The doctrine whereof is to be preached by every minister of the gospel as well as that of faith in Christ."

Evangelical grace, how often do we see a term like that? It's not a common way to express a concept like this, but it's not a wasted word either. It can be easy to gloss over something like that as just old language, but if we explore it, it can give us a little deeper foundation of what we're going to be looking at.

Merriam-Webster defines evangelical as "of relating to or being in agreement with the Christian gospel, especially as it is presented in the four gospels." That's valid enough, but we could do better than that. The Greek, *ewangelion*, appears in the New Testament as good news and used as gospel. Therefore, based on that verbiage and its use, it's not a stretch to say that we could term this doctrine a gospel grace. It's not merely aligning with the gospel, but is a gift from God that is integral to the plan of salvation that is unfolded to us in the gospel.

As a component of God's gift, the very opportunity to repent itself is a gift within a gift. In the larger catechism, questions 76 and 87, we see the term "saving grace," which is more familiar than evangelical grace. In his commentary on the larger catechism, Vos writes of the phrase saving grace: "It is called saving because its outcome is salvation or eternal life. It is called a grace because it is something we receive as a gift from God, not something we have naturally of ourselves."

### Repentance for All the Elect

Acts 10 and 11 shows us that this gift has been distributed to all the elect under the New Covenant. Jews and Gentiles alike are granted the privilege and opportunity to repent unto life.

Acts 10 gives us the backstory of a man named Cornelius. God had reached him and his family in some capacity, but they had not yet heard the gospel as preached by the apostles. As you might infer by his name, Cornelius was not a Jew. He was as Italian as they come. He was the commanding officer over a detachment of Italian-born soldiers stationed in a port city northwest of Jerusalem. And yet this was the man to whom Peter was summoned to preach the fullness of the good news at that moment. They dropped everything, came up from Joppa and ministered to Cornelius and his family.

The dialogue that this teaching opportunity sparked with the crowds outside reveals the words by which Cornelius and all his household were saved. Acts 11:17-18:

> "If therefore God gave them the same gift as he gave us when we believed on the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could withstand God? When they heard these things, they became silent and they glorified God saying, Then God has also granted the Gentiles repentance to life."

It's actually the only place in Scripture where we see "repentance to life" written out as such. God went out of his way to show that the Gentiles are folded into the New Covenant and that salvation, and therefore repentance unto life is open to all. He fills his minister—the spirit fills his minister—with these words: repentance to life, and the crowd obviously picks up on that theme and is able to articulate it back.

Vos expounds on this correlation in his catechism commentary. How is the repentance unto life wrought in the heart of a sinner? By the spirit and word of God. Here the term "word of God" means not only the Bible, but the message of saving truth contained in the Bible. That is the gospel of Jesus Christ, regardless of whether it is read, preached, or proclaimed in some other way. Vos implies that the doctrine of repentance is a package deal with gospel truth. This is what the divines are communicating, though using far fewer words.

The countless passages along the lines of "repent for the kingdom of God is at hand" ought to be exegeted just as thoroughly as John 3:16 or Romans 3:23. The idea of preaching repentance is exactly what the Westminster Assembly addresses in the next point of paragraph one.

### Preaching Repentance and Faith Together

**"Preached by every minister of the gospel as well as that of faith in Christ."**

Mark 6:11 and 12 says, verse 12 is about as clear of a proof text as you can get for that point. The spirit recorded this for a reason. The primary objective was the repentance of those who heard. It was the focal point of this preaching tour that he sent the twelve out on. The core teaching of these disciples must have highlighted the holiness of God, the disgust he has for sin, and the human position in redemptive history with the kingdom of God close at hand.

Viewing verse 11 in light of verse 12 reveals an unsettling thought, though. Christ says that a fate worse than Sodom and Gomorrah awaits those who refuse to come to terms with their sin and pursue repentance. Christ will shake them off just as his disciples would shake off the dust from the city that clings to their sandals. If this passage cannot cultivate an attitude of repentance, I don't think much else will.

The confession instructs that repentance be preached, but how it is preached matters too. You cannot have faith without repentance. You cannot have repentance without faith. You can't have one without the other. Repentance is just as much an element of Christ saving us as election or generation or obedience.

1 John 1:6 and 9 through 10:

> "If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar and his word is not in us."

Living in light requires repentance that we may be strengthened and drawn out of darkness. Faith without repentance is falsehood and repentance without faith is fruitless.

### Repentance and Confession Distinguished

A final point of distinction before we move on is that we ought not to confuse repentance and confession. Confession is an integral component of repentance, but there are nuances to this gospel grace that require some consideration here. Teaching faith and confession is insufficient to satisfy the goal of paragraph 1's instruction. Confession and repentance are not exactly the same.

Confession is simply an action, whether in prayer or in person, of owning up to a specific sin. We see murderers in the courtroom that will confess their crime with sort of depraved glee in their eyes. No hint of desire to acknowledge their moral turpitude or to course correct. Technically, there are no strings attached to confession. A heart could confess to another person without any thought of repentance.

This is what the Assembly is getting way out in front of in this chapter. It's a core reason why teaching a full understanding of repentance, not just confession, unto life is critical from the pulpit.

## Paragraph Three: Repentance Not as Satisfaction for Sin

**Paragraph Three:** "Although repentance be not to be rested in as any satisfaction for sin or any cause of the pardon thereof, which is the act of God's free grace in Christ, yet it is of such necessity to all sinners that none may expect pardon without it."

In his antidote to the Council of Trent on Justification, canon 11, from 1547, John Calvin puts forth this proposition. I'm sure we've all heard a paraphrase of it before: "It is therefore, faith alone which justifies, and yet the faith which justifies is not alone."

I believe that sentiment is exactly what the confession is trying to echo in this paragraph. We should not rest in the doctrine of repentance as satisfaction of sin for one primary reason. The doctrine of repentance did not die on the cross as satisfaction for our sins. Jesus Christ did so that we might believe and turn to him and glorify his Father.

In this vein, Vos poses the question: if repentance cannot cancel our sins, then why must we repent? The answer: Christ came to this world not simply to save us, but to save us from sin. He came not simply to give us eternal life, but to give us eternal righteousness. We cannot accept a part of what Christ offers. We must take all or nothing. If we do not want righteousness, then we cannot have eternal life either. We cannot be saved without being saved from sin.

The person who does not repent is the person who wants to hold on to sin. This state of mind is contrary to accepting Christ as our savior from sin. We cannot have our sins and also have our salvation from our sins at the same time, any more than a person could be saved from fire while deliberately remaining in a burning building.

As we saw when we defined our terms, repentance is the inward and outward action of turning ourselves towards godliness. It is not, however, the cause of pardon, as the confession says. So we ought not to rest assured if we hear the gospel grace and do nothing in response.

Christ himself, two times back to back in Luke 13:3 and 5 says:

> "But unless you repent, you will all likewise perish."

That's pretty black and white. Saying, "Thanks Lord, often I see you, much appreciated," and moving on with life in sin is like tying the millstone to our own necks. The same can be said of viewing repentance as our way to wow the Lord with our dedication that we might be led into heaven.

I'll let Chad Vendixhorn take this one:

> "Here the basic point is that we ought not to think that our change in attitude and action impresses the Lord, a message which the Lord passed on more than once through his prophet Ezekiel. The covenant Lord declared to the prophet that he was going to show mercy to his wayward people. He was going to give them a new heart and cause them to walk in his statutes and keep his laws. These people were going to be transformed, but they needed to remember that God was not doing it for their sakes. That is not for anything they had done or were about to do. He was helping them in spite of themselves and only because he's merciful. Their only appropriate stance was shame for sinful ways and gratitude for the Lord's mercy."

In a few short words, if Christ is the heartbeat of our faith, then I would venture to say that repentance is the breathing lung. Without a repentant heart, aware of sin and striving to rise above it, we will not have a living, breathing walk with our Savior. To tie our definition back in, unless we change our mind and purpose, regret and lament our sins and turn again to pursuing holiness, that so-called faith we might have is effectively lifeless.

## Paragraph Four: The Scope of Divine Mercy

**Paragraph Four:** "As there is no sin so small, but it deserves damnation, so there is no sin so great that it can bring damnation upon those who truly repent."

1 John 1:5 says:

> "This is the message which we have heard from him and declare to you that God is light and in him is no darkness at all."

God is light, God is pure holiness and goodness. Darkness and the opposition to holiness that embodies has no place before God in his realm. The darkness must be driven away; it's required by God's nature.

In the ESV, the Gospel of John chapter 1 verse 5 is translated:

> "The light shines in the darkness and the darkness has not overcome it."

The language here evokes a constant losing battle that the Prince of Darkness is waging on the Lord of Light. It is a battle that he will continue to fight on the losing end until the fulfillment of Revelation 21. God's goodness, his light, is everlasting. As the confession shows us in paragraph 4, this is cause for great encouragement, but not without an equal dose of concern for our sin.

Vos puts it succinctly: "Sin is not a trifle nor a slight evil, it is absolutely evil so that any sin, even the least, deserves God's wrath and curse to all eternity. Even the least sin is a total contradiction of God's holiness. Therefore, the Christian throughout life must always have a deep sorrow for sin."

Numbers 14:18 reads:

> "The Lord is longsuffering and abundant in mercy, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he by no means clears the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation."

God is jealous of the honor that he is shorted when iniquity is committed and not repented of. Same side of the coin though, he will gladly forgive iniquity and transgression when they are repented of.

### No Sin Too Great for Forgiveness

The second half of paragraph 4 states that there is no sin so great that it can bring damnation upon those who truly repent. I believe Hosea 14:1-6 illustrates this point and goes beyond within our theme.

Verse 1: When the people of God heed the call to drop and turn from their political and military and material idolatry, and in verse 4, the Lord replies with mercy and forgiveness.

When the people of God heed the call to drop and turn from their political and military and material idolatry, we find that God is merciful to forgive completely. His anger has turned away, but damnation the people deserve is happily withheld by a God who accepts true repentance.

Let's stop and bask in these words. We as the people of God under the New Covenant are promised these things here as well. God who would be just to eliminate any backslider simply on principle of his holiness will heal his offenders, heal the backsliders. When we pursue true repentance, God won't just hold off damnation. He will mend our sin-broken hearts that we might be more like him.

Second, he will love us freely. Imagine that our Heavenly Father who is love, freely loving repentance seekers. Not just a sprinkle of love here and there, but a free flowing flood of love that we might love him, his son and his people all the more.

Third, we find this analogy of trees. We see strength with roots and branches. We see prosperity with olives and lilies, but the core here is new life, new growth, new beauty, new strength wrought by a loving and holy God. It is God who grants the repentance and is he also who grants the new life.

Chapter 15 of the confession shouts the message of Hosea 14 from the rooftops: repentance unto life by the loving, redemptive plan of our Heavenly Father.

## Closing Encouragement

With an understanding of this doctrine as a cornerstone, Lord willing, next week we will look more in depth at what applied repentance looks like internally and externally in the private and public realms.

Until then, I'll close out with one final encouragement from Van Dixhorn:

> "Are you stained with sin that you cannot wash away? Then look to the grace of God in Christ and repent of your sins. If you do, you will surely find a gracious redemption that is full and free."

Any questions can be directed to Tito Lyro at OlympiaBP.net. You'll get some really great answers out of that.
